abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: First‐line atezolizumab combination therapies were approved for the treatment of metastatic non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) based on results from the global phase 3 trials IMpower130, IMpower132, and IMpower150. These trials reported 12‐month overall survival (OS) rates of 60%–67% with atezolizumab combination therapy. J‐TAIL‐2 (NCT04501497), a prospective, multicenter, observational study, evaluated atezolizumab combination therapy in routine clinical practice in Japan. Patients ≥ 20 years old with NSCLC received atezolizumab plus carboplatin and nab‐paclitaxel (atezo + CnP), atezolizumab plus carboplatin or cisplatin plus pemetrexed (atezo + PP), or atezolizumab plus bevacizumab plus carboplatin and paclitaxel (atezo + bev + CP) in clinical practice. The primary endpoint was the 12‐month OS rate. Secondary endpoints included OS, progression‐free survival, and subgroup analyses, including IMpower‐unlike (did not meet the main eligibility criteria of each IMpower trial) and IMpower‐like patients. In total, 814 patients were enrolled (atezo + CnP, n = 217; atezo + PP, n = 211; atezo + bev + CP, n = 386). The IMpower‐unlike group included patients with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≥ 2, autoimmune disease, or interstitial lung disease. Twelve‐month OS rates (95% confidence interval [CI]) were 62.9% (55.8–69.2), 72.1% (65.2–77.9), and 68.3% (63.2–72.9) with atezo + CnP, atezo + PP, and atezo + bev + CP, respectively. OS hazard ratios (95% CI) in the IMpower‐unlike vs. ‐like subgroups were 1.36 (0.91–2.05), 1.08 (0.70–1.68), and 1.49 (1.09–2.06), respectively. No new safety signals were observed. Real‐world efficacy and safety for each atezolizumab combination were comparable to those in the relevant IMpower trials.

sec.p: Keywords: atezolizumab, chemotherapy, lung cancer, non‐small cell, observational

abstract.p: The J‐TAIL‐2 prospective, observational study evaluated atezolizumab combined with several chemotherapy regimens in patients with advanced/metastatic non‐small cell lung cancer in routine clinical practice in Japan. The real‐world efficacy and safety of each atezolizumab combination were found to be comparable to those seen in the relevant global, randomized trials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The prognosis for metastatic non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains poor, with a 5‐year survival rate of less than 10% [1]. Regimens combining immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with chemotherapy have now become established treatment approaches for metastatic NSCLC. These include the combination of atezolizumab, an anti–programmed death‐ligand 1 (PD‐L1) monoclonal antibody, with different chemotherapy regimens.

First‐line atezolizumab combination therapies were approved for the treatment of metastatic NSCLC based on the results of the global phase 3 IMpower130 [2], IMpower132 [3], and IMpower150 [4] trials. In IMpower130, a significant improvement in overall survival (OS) and progression‐free survival (PFS) was seen with first‐line atezolizumab plus carboplatin and nab‐paclitaxel (atezo + CnP) treatment vs. chemotherapy alone [2]. In IMpower132, first‐line treatment with atezolizumab plus carboplatin or cisplatin plus pemetrexed (atezo + PP) resulted in significantly improved PFS and numerically improved OS vs. PP alone [3]. Additionally, IMpower150 showed that the addition of atezolizumab to bevacizumab plus carboplatin and paclitaxel (atezo + bev + CP) significantly improved PFS and OS in patients with non‐squamous NSCLC who had not previously received chemotherapy [4].

Many patients with common real‐world background factors were excluded from the IMpower studies based on their eligibility criteria (including patients with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status [ECOG PS] of ≥ 2, those with a history of autoimmune disease or interstitial lung disease [ILD], and those with brain metastases). It remains unknown whether the presence of these baseline characteristics affects the efficacy and safety of atezolizumab combination therapy.

J‐TAIL‐2 (NCT04501497) is a prospective observational study conducted to collect real‐world clinical information in patients with NSCLC or extensive‐stage small cell lung cancer (ES‐SCLC) treated with atezolizumab combination therapy in Japan. We report the results from the NSCLC cohort of J‐TAIL‐2, which examined the effectiveness and safety of three atezolizumab combination therapies in patients treated in clinical practice, including patients who would not have met the eligibility criteria for the relevant IMpower clinical trials.

sec.title: Study Design and Patient Population
sec.p: This multicenter, noninterventional, prospective observational study enrolled two cohorts of patients (NSCLC and ES‐SCLC) across 150 institutions in Japan. Eligible patients for the NSCLC cohort were aged ≥ 20 years and were scheduled to begin atezolizumab combination therapy (atezo + CnP, atezo + PP, or atezo + bev + CP) to treat NSCLC in clinical practice. The atezo + CnP, atezo + PP, and atezo + bev + CP regimens were previously evaluated in the IMpower130 [2], IMpower132 [3], and IMpower150 [4] trials, respectively. Patients for whom participation in this clinical research was not appropriate as deemed by their attending physician were not included. Each drug was administered according to its local labels (dosage and schedule). Subsequent therapy after discontinuation or completion of study treatment and criteria for dose reduction, interruption, or discontinuation were not specified.

J‐TAIL‐2 was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, and the Ethical Guidelines for Medical and Health Research Involving Human Subjects. Enrolled patients received a full explanation of the clinical research and provided written consent to participate. The Ethics Review Committee of each study site approved the study protocol and the informed consent form prior to study initiation at the site.

sec.title: Endpoints and Assessments
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the 12‐month OS rate, defined as the proportion of patients alive at 12 months among all OS rates, estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method at each time point. Secondary endpoints included OS, PFS, objective response rate (ORR), and incidence of adverse events (AEs). OS was defined as the time from the first day of study treatment until death from any cause with censoring. Surviving patients and patients lost to follow‐up were censored at the last contact date, and patients without post‐baseline information were censored at the day after the first day of study treatment. PFS was assessed by the investigator per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 and defined as the time from the first day of study treatment until first disease progression or death from any cause.

Effectiveness and safety analyses were conducted in select subgroups based on characteristics at the time of enrollment, including IMpower‐unlike vs. ‐like, ECOG PS ≥ 2 vs. < 2, with vs. without history or complication of autoimmune disease, with vs. without brain metastasis, with vs. without epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, and others. Patient subgroups were defined as IMpower‐like if they met the eligibility criteria based on IMpower130, IMpower132, or IMpower150 (Table S1) and as IMpower‐unlike if they would not have met the eligibility criteria shown in Table S1.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The target sample size for the NSCLC cohort was set as 800 patients based on feasibility, with consideration of factors such as the enrollment period and the number of enrollment sites. Based on the difference in 12‐month OS rates between the Phase 3 OAK trial and the real‐world TAIL study, and the 12‐month OS rates of the IMpower130, IMpower132, IMpower150 trials, the 12‐month OS rate for this study was assumed to be 56.7% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 53.3–60.2).

Under these assumptions, the recruitment of 800 patients in the NSCLC cohort would enable a reasonably accurate estimation of the 12‐month OS rate in a patient population that reflects the real‐world clinical setting in Japan. A maximum enrollment for each regimen was not predefined to ensure that enrollment into each regimen reflected real‐world treatment patterns for the relevant atezolizumab combination.

Effectiveness endpoints were calculated in the efficacy analysis population, defined as all treated patients who met eligibility criteria. Median OS, PFS, and survival rates at various timepoints were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methodology. The Brookmeyer–Crowley method was used to calculate 95% CIs for median OS and PFS; Greenwood's formula was used to calculate 95% CIs for survival rates at various timepoints.

Incidence and severity of AEs were summarized using National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v5.0 grades in the safety analysis population. The safety analysis population included all enrolled patients who received ≥ 1 dose of atezolizumab or bevacizumab (for patients receiving the atezo + bev + CP regimen only).

sec.title: Patients and Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: From August 21, 2020, to February 3, 2022, 814 patients were enrolled in the intention‐to‐treat (ITT) population, including 217 patients receiving atezo + CnP, 211 patients receiving atezo + PP, and 386 patients receiving atezo + bev + CP (Figure S1). The data cutoff date was February 3, 2023. The safety analysis population comprised 800 patients (atezo + CnP, n = 216; atezo + PP, n = 205; atezo + bev + CP, n = 379), and the efficacy analysis population comprised 791 patients (atezo + CnP, n = 208; atezo + PP, n = 204; atezo + bev + CP, n = 379).

Baseline characteristics of the ITT population are shown in Table 1. Median age at enrollment was 69 years (range, 32–85); 21.5% (n = 175) were ≥ 75 years old, 69.8% (n = 568) were male, and 74.3% (n = 605) were current or former smokers. In the overall ITT population, 4.2% (n = 34) had concurrent ILD and 3.9% (n = 32) had concurrent autoimmune disease. Of 800 patients in the safety analysis population, 66.6% (n = 533) were IMpower‐unlike at baseline. Among patients treated with atezo + CnP, a lower proportion had adenocarcinoma histology and a higher proportion had PD‐L1 expression on ≥ 50% of tumor cells relative to patients receiving other regimens. Among patients treated with atezo + bev + CP, a lower proportion were ≥ 75 years or male, and the proportion of current/previous smokers was relatively lower (≥ 10% difference) than that in patients receiving other regimens. A greater proportion of patients in the atezo + bev + CP group had EGFR mutations and brain metastases than in other groups. In the efficacy analysis population, 194/379 patients receiving atezo + bev + CP had EGFR mutations. Although advanced vs. perioperative treatment was not differentiated, 182/194 patients (93.8%) had been previously treated with any EGFR‐tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), while only 12/194 patients (6.2%) had not been treated with EGFR‐TKIs. Baseline characteristics of the safety analysis population are shown in Table S2, reflecting the patients in the IMpower‐unlike subgroup who would not have met eligibility criteria for the IMpower trials.

sec.title: Effectiveness
sec.p: The median observation time was 14.1 months (range, 0.1–28.3) in the overall efficacy analysis population. OS, PFS, and ORR data in the overall population and by regimen are summarized in Table 2. In the efficacy analysis population, 12‐month OS rates (95% CI) were 62.9% (55.8–69.2), 72.1% (65.2–77.9), and 68.3% (63.2–72.9), and median OS (95% CI) was 19.7 (16.1–25.9), 23.5 (17.7–not estimable [NE]), and 17.3 (15.6–19.9) months in patients receiving atezo + CnP, atezo + PP and atezo + bev + CP, respectively (Table 2; Figure 1A,B). Median PFS (95% CI) was 5.6 months (5.1–6.9) with atezo + CnP, 7.0 months (5.5–8.3) with atezo + PP, and 6.3 months (5.7–6.7) with atezo + bev + CP (Table 2; Figure 1C,D). Twelve‐month PFS rates (95% CI) were 28.7% (22.6–35.0), 31.0% (24.7–37.5), and 20.9% (17.0–25.2), respectively. ORR (95% CI) was 47.4% (40.2–54.7) with atezo + CnP, 41.9% (34.8–49.4) with atezo + PP, and 44.2% (38.6–49.8), with atezo + bev + CP (Table 2).

sec.p: In the IMpower‐unlike vs. ‐like subgroups, median OS was 17.7 vs. 25.9 months with atezo + CnP (hazard ratio [HR], 1.36; 95% CI: 0.91–2.05), 23.5 vs. 20.6 months with atezo + PP (HR, 1.08; 95% CI: 0.70–1.68), and 16.4 vs. 21.9 months with atezo + bev + CP (HR, 1.49; 95% CI: 1.09–2.06; Figure S2). OS and PFS outcomes for additional select subgroups are summarized in Figures 2 and S3. PD‐L1 ≥ 50% HRs for OS tended to be better than those for PD‐L1 < 1% across regimens, similar to previous reports (Figure S4) [2, 3, 5].

sec.p: Shorter OS and PFS were seen in subgroups with ECOG PS ≥ 2 vs. < 2 and those with vs. without EGFR mutations. In the ECOG PS ≥ 2 vs. < 2 subgroups, median OS was 6.2 vs. 20.8 months in the atezo + CnP group (HR, 2.42; 95% CI: 1.45–4.04), 6.6 vs. 25.7 months in the atezo + PP group (HR, 4.71; 95% CI: 2.50–8.87), and 6.9 vs. 17.7 months in the atezo + bev + CP group (HR, 2.15; 95% CI: 1.28–3.61; Figure S5). In the subgroup analysis by ECOG PS, the mOS of patients with ECOG PS 2 was 8.3 months for atezo + CP, 6.7 months for atezo + PP, and 6.9 months for atezo + bev + CP and the mPFS was 2.9, 3.9, and 3.4 months, respectively (Figure S6). Among patients receiving atezo + bev + CP, median OS was 15.7 months in the EGFR mutation‐positive subgroup (comprising 194 [51.2%] efficacy‐evaluable patients) and 18.8 months in the EGFR mutation‐negative subgroup (HR, 1.23; 95% CI: 0.92–1.66); median PFS was 5.8 vs. 7.6 months (HR, 1.63; 95% CI: 1.30–2.04; Figure S7).

Median OS in the presence vs. absence of brain metastases subgroups was 16.7 vs. 19.8 months (HR 1.13; 95% CI: 0.71–1.80) in the atezo + CnP group, 16.3 vs. 25.7 months (HR, 1.59; 95% CI: 0.97–2.61) in the atezo + PP group, and 16.6 vs. 18.1 months (HR, 1.23; 95% CI: 0.91–1.66) in the atezo + bev + CP group (Figure S8). In the with vs. without autoimmune disease subgroups, median OS was 19.8 vs. 19.4 months (HR, 0.86; 95% CI: 0.35–2.12) in the atezo + CnP group, 23.5 vs. 24.0 months (HR, 0.94; 95% CI: 0.35–2.57) in the atezo + PP group, and 22.5 vs. 17.1 months (HR, 0.72; 95% CI: 0.34–1.52) in the atezo + bev + CP group (Figure S9).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: In the safety analysis population (n = 800), any grade AEs occurred in 87.6% (n = 701), Grade ≥ 3 AEs in 60.4% (n = 483), and Grade 5 AEs in 1.3% of patients (n = 10; Table 3). Grade ≥ 3 AEs occurred in 60.6% of patients receiving atezo + CnP, 48.3% receiving atezo + PP, and 66.8% receiving atezo + bev + CP. Any grade immune‐related AEs occurred in 231 patients overall (28.9%) and 30.8% of patients with autoimmune disease. The most common AEs are shown in Table S3.

sec.p: Safety outcomes were generally consistent across select subgroups (Table S4). In the IMpower‐unlike vs. ‐like subgroups, the incidence of Grade ≥ 3 AEs (61.2% vs. 58.8%) and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation (12.8% vs. 14.2%) were similar. Adverse drug reactions associated with atezolizumab occurred in 29.7% of patients with ECOG PS ≥ 2 vs. 42.8% of patients with ECOG < 2. Serious AEs occurred in 17.9% of patients with a history of autoimmune disease vs. 35.0% of patients without.

A total of 64 patients (8.0%) developed ILD, which resulted in death in two patients (0.3%; Table S5). Incidences of ILD by regimen were 11.6% for atezo + CnP, 11.7% for atezo + PP, and 4.0% for atezo + bev + CP. Among patients with ILD (excluding radiation pneumonitis) at baseline (n = 25), five patients (20.0%) had worsening ILD, which resulted in one death (4%); all five patients received atezo + CnP. Among patients with radiation pneumonitis at baseline (n = 9), one patient (11.1%) who received atezo + CnP had worsening ILD (Grade 2).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This prospective observational study supports the use of atezolizumab combined with chemotherapy in patients with NSCLC in Japanese clinical practice. The patient population in the J‐TAIL‐2 NSCLC cohort was distinct from a trial population. Approximately two‐thirds of the patients enrolled in this real‐world study would not have met the eligibility criteria of the IMpower130 [2], IMpower132 [3], and IMpower150 studies [4]. Results of this study indicate that atezolizumab combination therapy remains efficacious and well tolerated in patients who would have been ineligible for the respective clinical trials.

A greater proportion of patients receiving atezo + bev + CP had EGFR mutations and brain metastases compared with those receiving other regimens, and adenocarcinoma histology was most common in patients receiving atezo + PP. These patient backgrounds suggest that in clinical practice the atezolizumab combination regimen is selected for a patient based on the characteristics of the combination drugs (such as pemetrexed and bevacizumab) [6, 7, 8].

Although cross‐trial comparisons should be made with caution given differences in study design and populations, it appeared that effectiveness in J‐TAIL‐2 was similar to that in the IMpower130 [2], IMpower132 [3], and IMpower150 studies [4]. Median OS in J‐TAIL‐2 was 19.7 months with atezo + CnP, 23.5 months with atezo + PP, and 17.3 months with atezo + bev + CP. In the IMpower trials [2, 3, 4, 9], median OS was 18.6 months in IMpower130, 17.5 months in IMpower132, and 19.8 months in IMpower150 with atezolizumab combination treatment. Notably, median OS with atezo + bev + CP reported in this real‐world study was similar to that seen in the IMpower150 trial despite differences in baseline EGFR mutation status between the two populations. Over 50% of patients receiving atezo + bev + CP in J‐TAIL‐2 had EGFR mutation‐positive NSCLC compared with only 9% of patients in IMpower150 [4].

Despite a limited median observation period of 14.1 months, the 12‐month PFS rates seen in J‐TAIL‐2 also appeared to be comparable to those observed in the IMpower130 [2], IMpower132 [3], and IMpower150 trials [4]. The 24‐month PFS rate in the overall population of J‐TAIL‐2 was 13.5%, indicating that a durable response could be obtained in a subset of patients in clinical practice.

Patients who received atezo + bev + CP had the lowest median OS and PFS relative to the patients receiving other regimens in this study. Although direct comparison of efficacy between regimens is inappropriate given the observational nature of this investigation in actual clinical settings, the lower efficacy rates of this group may have multiple explanations. The atezo + bev + CP regimen enrolled 34.5% of patients with brain metastases at baseline, which is associated with poor prognosis [10]. This percentage is higher than that for atezo + CnP (20.3%) and atezo + PP (21.3%). Additionally, the majority (52.5%) of patients who received atezo + bev + CP had EGFR mutation‐positive disease. Of those patients with EGFR mutations who were efficacy‐evaluable, 93.8% had previously been treated with EGFR‐TKI, although data were not available for whether therapy was given in the advanced or perioperative setting. Given the high incidence of these baseline characteristics associated with poor outcomes, the median OS and PFS with atezo + bev + CP may have been numerically lower than other regimens.

Median OS with atezo + bev + CP was numerically lower in the EGFR mutation–positive vs. EGFR mutation–negative group (15.7 vs. 18.8 months; HR, 1.23; 95% CI: 0.92–1.66) of J‐TAIL‐2. It should be noted that this population includes patients who had received multiple lines of prior TKI therapy and/or chemotherapy. Therefore, despite the numerically lower OS seen in the EGFR mutation‐positive group in this study, atezo + bev + CP is a potential treatment option in this population. A recent phase 3 study in Korea showed that the atezo + bev + CP combination retained its clinical benefit in patients with EGFR‐ and ALK‐mutated NSCLC, with significant improvement in PFS and ORR with atezo + bev + CP vs. platinum‐based doublet chemotherapy alone [11]. Additionally, a subgroup analysis of the IMpower150 study also indicated that the OS and PFS benefits of atezo + bev + CP treatment were maintained in patients with EGFR‐positive NSCLC [12].

The atezo + bev + CP combination is an important treatment option in EGFR‐positive NSCLC due to the potential role of bevacizumab in altering the EGFR‐positive tumor microenvironment. The increased levels of VEGF expression in EGFR‐mutant tumors due to EGFR‐VEGF crosstalk may heighten the sensitivity of these tumors to bevacizumab [13, 14]. In contrast, several phase 2/3 studies have reported unsatisfactory efficacy following treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors, either as single agents or with other chemotherapy combinations, in EGFR‐positive NSCLC [15, 16, 17].

No new safety signals were observed in the safety analysis population of J‐TAIL‐2. The incidence of AEs leading to death was 1.3%, which was comparable among regimens and lower than rates reported in the IMpower trials (IMpower130: 5.3%; IMpower132: 7.9%; IMpower150: 5.9%) [2, 3, 4]. The incidence of AEs leading to study discontinuation was 13.3%, which was lower than that reported with atezolizumab combination therapy in the clinical trials (26.4% in IMpower130 [2], 28.5% in IMpower132 [3], and 32.6% in IMpower150 [4]). This may reflect the strict criteria for treatment discontinuation in clinical trials compared with the real‐world setting, where treatment can be optimized by physicians with potential modification of dose and/or schedule.

Incidence of ILD with atezo + bev + CP (4.0%) was similar to that reported in the IMpower150 trial (2.8%) [4] and was also lower than in the atezo + CnP (11.6%) and atezo + PP (11.7%) groups of this J‐TAIL‐2 study. A study using an IL‐2– and IL‐18–induced mouse pneumonitis model found that blocking PD‐1 signaling with anti–PD‐L1 and anti–PD‐L2 antibodies led to worsened pneumonitis [18]. However, aggravation of pneumonitis could be prevented by an anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antibody, which was shown to protect against the vascular‐to‐alveolar leakage caused by PD‐1 signal blockade. These results suggest that combining anti‐VEGF antibodies with checkpoint inhibitors may help control checkpoint inhibitor–related pneumonitis. This may explain the lower incidence of ILD with atezo + bev + CP compared with the other two regimens in this study.

Among the patients with ILD at baseline, 38.5% of patients receiving atezo + CnP had worsening ILD, compared with none of the patients receiving the other two regimens. More patients with ILD at baseline received atezo + CnP than the other two regimens, indicating that selection bias may impact these data. It is possible that physicians prefer to initiate atezo + CnP rather than atezo + bev + CP or atezo + PP for patients with ILD at baseline, which may explain the results observed in this analysis. Combination immunotherapy should be used with careful consideration in lung cancer patients with ILD at baseline.

Subgroup analysis data indicated that the incidence of AEs with atezolizumab combination therapy was similar in the IMpower‐unlike and ‐like populations. Furthermore, median OS in the IMpower‐unlike subgroups of J‐TAIL‐2 was similar to those seen with the respective treatment regimens in the IMpower clinical trials [2, 3, 4]. These data indicate that atezolizumab combination therapy can be effective and well‐tolerated in clinical practice, even in patients who do not meet clinical trial eligibility criteria. However, considering the relatively worse survival in patients with metastatic NSCLC who have ECOG PS ≥ 2 (Figure S6), an IMpower‐unlike characteristic, immune checkpoint inhibition plus chemotherapy should be administered with careful consideration of the risks and benefits. The incidence of immune‐related AEs and ILD was comparable between patients with and without autoimmune disease, indicating that atezolizumab combination therapy may be tolerable in this population.

Limitations of the J‐TAIL‐2 study include its observational nature and the lack of a control group. Additionally, the frequency of imaging assessments was not specified and may have varied across participating sites. Detailed data on the status of autoimmune disease, ILD and brain metastases present at baseline were not collected, limiting the interpretation of results in these subgroups.

In conclusion, the large observational J‐TAIL‐2 study of patients with NSCLC in clinical practice in Japan showed that the effectiveness of atezolizumab combination therapy was consistent with that reported in the IMpower130, IMpower132, and IMpower150 trials. There were no new safety signals identified, and subgroup analyses showed an acceptable benefit–risk profile in patients with comorbidities who would have been ineligible for the IMpower clinical trials.
